segments.title: Reading a treaty through its delegates
segments.summary: Who each government sent to Washington reveals its priorities and whether the resulting treaty could win support at home.
segments.body: The conference is approached like a warship design: stated objectives matter, but the people selected reveal the real priorities and trade-offs. The Dutch 1913-14 battleship tender provides the comparison, since British and German yards answered the same requirement with different design emphases. Signatory delegates had unusual leverage because they could shape negotiations, report back to their governments, and decide whether to put their names to the result. Other specialists could advise them, but could not commit a state in the same way. This method makes the treaty terms intelligible as political choices instead of an abstract balance-sheet exercise.

evidence.note: The lecture explains its delegate-focused method and the special influence of signatories.

segments.title: American status, spending, and Senate ratification
segments.summary: The American delegation sought global recognition and a cheaper alternative to competing capital-ship programmes.
segments.body: The discussion links Charles Evans Hughes, Henry Cabot Lodge, Oscar Underwood, and Elihu Root to both executive policy and Senate approval. The United States wanted parity in global standing with Britain while avoiding the cost of an unchecked naval contest, particularly where Japanese construction could compel further American building. Root supplied a public peace-and-disarmament rationale, while Hughes represented the administration's bargaining power. Sending both the Senate majority and minority leaders helped turn an international settlement into one that could pass domestically.

evidence.note: The transcript sets out American status, cost, Japanese-construction, and Senate-ratification aims.

segments.title: Industrial capacity behind American arms control
segments.summary: American acceptance of limits rested on the ability to outbuild Japan if necessary, while a treaty offered the same security at much lower cost.
segments.body: Britain, the United States, and Japan were competing over warship quality and technology, while German naval laws had emphasized ship numbers for a risk-fleet strategy. Britain's industrial capabilities and export market rewarded continued technical competition. American political enthusiasm for continuous construction had weakened, yet the country's industrial base could still outproduce Japan. Japanese building was the immediate pressure that might force Congress to fund more ships. A treaty limiting that construction let Washington save money and secure formal equality with Britain, so arms control rested on industrial strength.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts qualitative competition, American production capacity, Japanese building pressure, and the savings offered by treaty limits.

segments.title: British disarmament ideals and imperial cruiser needs
segments.summary: Britain entered seeking peace and economy, but would not accept limits that prevented it from policing a global empire with cruisers.
segments.body: David Lloyd George hoped disarmament could reduce the chance of another continental catastrophe, but Britain still had to defend far-flung routes and possessions. It could accept capital-ship constraints and wanted replacements for older battleships, yet it resisted numerical cruiser limits. The imperial plan expected Dominion cruiser squadrons to patrol sea lanes and counter surface raiders. The treaty therefore limited cruiser size rather than total numbers, with the Hawkins class supplying the benchmark. The unrealised programme called for 40-48 County-class cruisers, with roughly 18-23 intended for the Dominions. This preserved room for a dispersed force even though most Dominions did not build on the scale London imagined.

evidence.note: The transcript covers postwar disarmament hopes, imperial commitments, the Hawkins-class size benchmark, and Britain's insistence on unrestricted cruiser numbers.
The closing prompt gives the proposed County-class construction range and the approximate Dominion allocation.

segments.title: Treaty limits and the problem of enforcement
segments.summary: Arms limits require more than signatures: governments must judge whether a violation is serious enough to enforce at real political cost.
segments.body: Using a hypothetical Italian cruiser built one thousand tons overweight, the video asks whether Britain or the United States would actually risk war to enforce a technical breach. Leaders would have to justify lives, taxes, and treasure to voters over a disputed displacement figure. That political test exposes the weakness of an agreement lacking an impartial and credible enforcement power. Durable limits therefore had to remain in each participant's self-interest rather than relying on signatures alone.

evidence.note: The transcript develops the enforcement problem through an example of a cruiser exceeding its treaty displacement.

segments.title: Dominion security depended on the Royal Navy
segments.summary: Canada, Australia, and New Zealand wanted different levels of local naval effort, but all had a stake in a strong Royal Navy.
segments.body: Canada is presented as willing to contribute money and supplies while avoiding the expense of a substantial peacetime fleet. Australia sought stronger local forces because maritime communications and widely separated population centres made sea power central to its security. New Zealand, with less population and fewer resources, depended even more directly on British naval strength. Those different circumstances still produced a united Commonwealth position against numerical cruiser limits because each Dominion relied on British ships to cover risks it could not meet alone.

evidence.note: The lecture compares Dominion resources, local forces, and reliance on the Royal Navy.

segments.title: Canadian economy versus visible deterrence
segments.summary: Canada could promise great wartime potential, but only ships already in service would create an immediate peacetime deterrent.
segments.body: Theoretical mobilization capacity did not have the deterrent effect of visible warships already at sea. A Canadian capital-ship or cruiser force would have made the Dominion's contribution concrete to any potential opponent. Ottawa instead preferred financial and supply support while leaving much of the standing naval burden to Britain. The choice saved money in peace, but it also limited Canada's maritime institutions and left deterrence dependent on forces maintained elsewhere.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts paper mobilization potential with visible ships and explains Canada's preference for limited peacetime obligations.

segments.title: Australian sea security and competitive shipbuilding
segments.summary: Australia's dispersed population and maritime trade made naval forces essential, while interwar yard competition made major ships more attainable than modern monopolies suggest.
segments.body: Capital ships were more than prestige purchases when multiple yards could compete to build them. Competition restrained prices in a way that a single-source carrier yard cannot, although public dockyards also require continuous work to remain economical. For Australia, the strategic case was unusually direct: the sea formed its defensive depth, its population centres could not easily support one another, and trade depended on maritime communications. Those conditions explain why Canberra wanted both its own flagship and unrestricted cruiser capacity rather than relying only on wartime promises.

evidence.note: The transcript links competitive yard economics to Australia's maritime geography, trade, and demand for naval strength.

segments.title: Why one Commonwealth navy mattered to the ratios
segments.summary: Treating the Dominions as part of one naval establishment prevented British strength from being multiplied through nominally separate fleets.
segments.body: Separate Dominion allowances could have made a formal capital-ship ratio misleading. Britain plus individual allowances for Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and India might have produced a much larger combined force than nominal Anglo-American parity suggested. Counting Commonwealth forces together closed that accounting route. It also bound Australia and New Zealand more tightly to the Royal Navy for security, showing how treaty ratios depended on constitutional definitions as much as ship totals.

evidence.note: The transcript examines the proposed treatment of Dominion capital ships within treaty ratios and the consequences of counting one Commonwealth navy.

segments.title: South Africa and the neglected Cape sea route
segments.summary: South Africa's sense of geographic safety obscured the naval importance of the Cape route and encouraged reliance on outside fleets.
segments.body: Jan Smuts's choice of Balfour was both a gesture of imperial trust and a way to remain detached from naval commitments. South Africa appeared remote from likely attackers, yet sat astride the diversion route that became vital whenever the Suez Canal or Mediterranean could not carry traffic. During the Second World War, South African air patrols and auxiliary vessels contributed, but the navy did not operate a Flower-class corvette until after the war. Local threat perceptions suppressed naval investment even though the country's waters were central to global logistics.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts South African remoteness and limited naval investment with the strategic importance of Cape shipping routes.

segments.title: India's navy as security and nation-building
segments.summary: The Indian naval case joins Indian Ocean security to the institutional value of a technically skilled, nationally mixed service.
segments.body: India needed naval power for its long coastlines, trade, and central position in the Indian Ocean. A navy could also mix communities aboard ship, reward technical competence, and help form a future national framework. The expected transition from empire to self-government would require institutions able to serve a nation-state. Indian political representatives and the Royal Navy could support expansion even when career administrators preferred other expenditure. Railways and other infrastructure competed for the same money. Such projects promised future wealth and growth, but they required immediate taxation or borrowing, so naval ambition had to fit wider development priorities.

evidence.note: The lecture connects India's coastal security, naval institutions, social mobility, and infrastructure constraints.

segments.title: French coalitions and fragmented shipbuilding
segments.summary: Rapid coalition turnover and independently minded yards made it harder for France to sustain coherent naval policy after the First World War.
segments.body: French governments could change as parliamentary coalitions were rearranged without a new general election, repeatedly shifting ministerial priorities. The naval industry had a parallel coordination problem because individual yards altered common plans and produced ships that were difficult to operate as a uniform squadron. This did not mean the yards built poor vessels, but it slowed completion and weakened standardization. Combined with wartime demographic and psychological losses, those institutional problems made an expensive race with Italy especially unattractive.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses unstable French coalitions, shipyard variation, and the political trauma left by the First World War.

segments.title: French disarmament required German weakness
segments.summary: French support for disarmament remained conditional on Germany being kept weaker, while Verdun's trauma made another continental war intolerable.
segments.body: French leaders did not treat disarmament as a willingness to accept equal vulnerability. President Alexandre Millerand and Raymond Poincare wanted French armament to remain above Germany's, while the Treaty of Versailles suppressed German maritime industry and naval capacity. Britain also accepted that reduction of German sea power even when the allies differed elsewhere. The losses and psychological trauma of Verdun made security against Germany inseparable from the desire to prevent another war. France could therefore favour arms limitation while demanding an unequal postwar order.

evidence.note: The transcript links Millerand and Poincare's disarmament policy to keeping Germany weaker, Versailles restrictions on German maritime industry, and the trauma of Verdun.

segments.title: France, Italy, and the cost of naval parity
segments.summary: French acceptance of parity with Italy created a mismatch between a Mediterranean fleet and France's wider colonial commitments.
segments.body: France wanted to avoid an expensive race with Italy after the trauma and losses of the First World War. Numerical parity nevertheless ignored France's dispersed commitments in Africa, the Caribbean, and the Far East. A fleet matched to Italy could cover the Mediterranean or protect overseas possessions, but not both simultaneously. Once French negotiators accepted parity, later bargaining could not repair the mismatch: France needed either parity with Japan or a margin over Italy. Dependence on Royal Navy support then shaped British planning and made the collapse or uncertain allegiance of French sea power especially consequential in the Second World War.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses French colonial commitments, Italian parity, dependence on British strength, and later wartime consequences.

segments.title: Italian parity and Mediterranean concentration
segments.summary: Italy needed only parity with France to concentrate superior strength in the Mediterranean while France divided attention across an empire.
segments.body: Ivanoe Bonomi and the Italian delegates recognized that equality in headline tonnage would favor the power with fewer worldwide commitments. Italy could focus on the Mediterranean while France either dispersed ships overseas or accepted local inferiority. With Austria-Hungary broken up and neither Greece nor the Ottoman state posing the same naval challenge, France was Italy's principal regional rival short of the Royal Navy. The aspiration to make the sea Mare Nostrum therefore predated Mussolini, although Bonomi still accounted for a continuing British presence. The delegation also included Luigi Albertini, whose later public opposition to Mussolini shows that interwar Italian politics retained meaningful institutional resistance as Fascism advanced. Italy could claim the treaty's only nominal victory, although the age of its ships kept that result from feeling like one.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Italy's concentration advantage, the older Mare Nostrum idea, and Albertini's later parliamentary opposition to Mussolini.
The closing comparison identifies Italy as the only nominal winner while noting the age of its ships.

segments.title: Japan's seven-to-ten risk-fleet logic
segments.summary: Japan sought a seven-to-ten ratio to make intervention costly, despite recognising that it could not sustain a long war with Britain or the United States.
segments.body: The proposed Japanese ratio was a deterrent calculation rather than a promise of outright victory. Japanese planners understood their industrial limits in a prolonged war against Britain or the United States, which helps explain their focus on short-war plans. Unlike Tirpitz's risk-fleet theory, the object was not to weaken an attacker for exploitation by a third power. Japan wanted enough strength to make conquest prohibitively difficult. The final 5:3 ratio largely preserved the existing balance, so Japan lost no established position but failed to gain the security its leaders sought.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Japan's desired ratio, industrial limits, short-war logic, and deterrent purpose.

segments.title: Japanese diplomacy and trans-Pacific miscommunication
segments.summary: Different diplomatic idioms turned Japanese attempts at explanation into apparent threats and deepened an already suspicious American relationship.
segments.body: British officials came somewhat closer to understanding Japanese diplomatic language because the alliance and long technical relationship had built more personal contact. American and French audiences had less shared context for Japanese illustrative phrasing. The later experience of Ambassador Masanao Hanihara, whose comments on American immigration legislation were read as a threat, demonstrates the danger. Translation skill mattered, but hostile listeners could also seize on ambiguity, allowing cultural and political suspicion to magnify disagreement.

evidence.note: The transcript connects Anglo-Japanese experience, differing diplomatic language, and the hostile interpretation of Hanihara's immigration statement.

segments.title: Equal ratios and unequal global commitments
segments.summary: Formal Anglo-American equality concealed the Royal Navy's wider geographic obligations and the tension between battle concentration and peacetime presence.
segments.body: The treaty matched Britain to a two-ocean United States even though the Royal Navy had major obligations in the Atlantic, Mediterranean, Indian Ocean, and Pacific. Capital ships could be concentrated for battle or dispersed to demonstrate commitment and deter conflict, but could not perform both tasks everywhere at once. This peacetime use of naval strength was conflict shaping rather than combat. Equal fleet totals therefore did not provide equal strategic capacity when geography and political commitments differed.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts British and American geographic commitments and the concentration-versus-presence problem for capital ships.

segments.title: How naval limits could deepen later fear
segments.summary: The closing argument is that naval disarmament could leave governments feeling too weak to act until they had rebuilt their fleets.
segments.body: The treaty left several powers dissatisfied with the forces available for their commitments. Because naval strength had been constrained while armies and air forces were not similarly limited, later expansion was naval rearmament rather than routine growth. Governments facing new threats could therefore delay action until they felt strong enough to intervene. Unlimited armament does not guarantee peace, but limits set below perceived security needs can produce fear instead of confidence.

evidence.note: The transcript links treaty constraints, later naval rearmament, delayed intervention, and deterrent confidence.

segments.title: Testing treaty arithmetic with an Australian capital ship
segments.summary: The closing prompt asks how a treaty could let Australia retain a capital ship and how that exception would reshape Dominion naval demands.
segments.body: The closing exercise is explicitly counterfactual rather than a claim about what the treaty provided. It asks what ratio or accounting system could have allowed Australia to keep a capital ship, which vessel might have survived, and how Canberra could have used it. The exception would also raise questions about whether Canada or India should receive comparable naval capacity. India might instead have gained the cruiser squadron envisaged in British planning. The proposed programme of 40-48 County-class cruisers, with roughly 18-23 intended for the Dominions, gives the exercise concrete force-structure stakes for testing how treaty arithmetic could reshape imperial burden-sharing.

evidence.note: The closing prompt asks viewers to construct a treaty system that preserves an Australian capital ship and to trace the consequences for Canadian and Indian forces and the planned County-class cruiser programme.
